8.2.6 Base-Load Nuclear Power

These two forms of generating capacity complement each other in the integrated power system and are not alternatives to each other. As more nuclear capacity is added to the system, a (nuclear) capacity level is eventually reached such that the system demand during off-peak hours is insufficient to keep all nuclear units loaded to, or near, full capacity. When this occurs, without sufficient energy-storage capacity (such as pumped storage) available, the load on at least some of the large low-production-cost nuclear units must be reduced to minimum or zero load.
A substantial period of time is required to bring the nuclear units from minimum load to full-load when the system demand increases and the output of these units is needed. This results in a loss of availability of the nuclear capacity which is costly, since the short-fall in capacity must be picked up by fast-response units such as combustion turbines with much higher production costs and high fossilfuel consumption. With sufficient pumped storage capacity available, the nuclear units may be maintained at full-load during off-peak hours by using their available capacity to supply pumping energy to the pumped storage unit. During peak-load hours the energy stored in this manner may be returned to the system to obviate the use of high production cost peaking units such as combustion turbines.
The production costs of nuclear base-load plants are so much lower than the production costs of fossil fueled peaking units that, when operating in conjunction with a pumped storage project, the total system cost and the total fossil fuel consumption for the system are reduced.
